topic.title: Algebraic fractions with linear denominators: adding, subtracting and solving equations
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: Two items most series, both in the last third of M4: a single-fraction question of 4–5 marks (Summer 2024 Q18(b), Summer 2025 Q21) and a fractional equation of 7–8 marks to 2 decimal places (Summer 2023 Q22, Summer 2024 Q23, November 2024 Q20, November 2025 Q24, Summer 2026 Q21). Simplify-and-cancel or factorise-then-divide items of 3–5 marks (November 2024 Q19, Summer 2025 Q20, November 2025 Q22, Summer 2026 Q16) test the same factorising.
mustMemorise: Common denominator = product of the two linear denominators, e.g. (x + 2)(2x − 1); multiply each numerator by the other denominator
A subtracted numerator stays in brackets; when the bracket goes, every sign inside it changes
A whole number n goes over the common denominator D as nD ÷ D
Factorise before cancelling; only whole factors cancel, never single terms; a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) in the order given
To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction, then factorise everything and cancel whole brackets

Equation: combine, multiply every term by the denominator in one line, expand, collect to ax² + bx + c = 0, factorise or use the formula with (−b)² bracketed, give both roots, reject a root only with a reason
onFormulaSheet: Quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a — given on the Higher sheet; needed when the cleared equation does not factorise
notOnThisSpec: Adding or subtracting fractions with a quadratic denominator (Teacher Guidance on M4-NA-03)
Equations with a quadratic denominator (Teacher Guidance on M4-NA-04)
Splitting a fraction into partial fractions (A level, not GCSE)

To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal

Equations with a quadratic denominator (Teacher Guidance on M4-NA-04)
Splitting a fraction into partial fractions (A level, not GCSE)

mustBeAbleTo: Add or subtract two algebraic fractions with linear denominators, e.g. 4/(x + 3) + 2/(3x − 1), giving one fraction with the denominator left as a product of brackets
Keep a subtracted numerator in brackets, expand it on one line, then change every sign when the bracket is removed
Include a whole number by writing it over the common denominator
Simplify a fraction by factorising top and bottom (common factor, grouping, difference of two squares) and cancelling whole factors
Multiply and divide algebraic fractions: invert the second fraction, factorise everything, cancel whole brackets
Clear the denominators of an equation such as 5/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 3) = 2, reach a quadratic, and solve by factorising or by the formula, giving both roots to the stated accuracy
Set up such an equation from a context (two journeys at x and x + 5 km/h) and reject a root only with a written reason
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). A single-fraction item of 4–5 marks (Summer 2024 Q18(b), Summer 2025 Q21) and, usually separately, a fractional equation of 7–8 marks with 'give your answers to 2 decimal places', placed among the last five questions (Summer 2023 Q22, Summer 2024 Q23, November 2024 Q20, November 2025 Q24, Summer 2026 Q21). Simplify-and-cancel or factorise-then-divide items of 3–5 marks sit at Q16–22 (November 2024 Q19, Summer 2025 Q20, November 2025 Q22, Summer 2026 Q16). Schemes give M1 A1 for the common denominator with correct numerators, then one MA1 per expansion or collection line; in an equation the two roots earn A1 each.
traps: Subtracting only the first term of a bracketed numerator — most candidates capped at 3 of 5 (Summer 2025 M4 Q21)
Leaving a whole number outside instead of writing it over the common denominator — under a tenth got full marks (Summer 2024 M4 Q18(b))
Multiplying the fractions by the denominator but not the constant on the other side, or moving a fraction across with the wrong sign (Summer 2024 M4 Q23, November 2024 M4 Q20)
Typing −b² without brackets in the formula so the discriminant comes out negative (November 2025 M4 Q24)
Dropping the second root when the question only says solve (Summer 2023 M4 Q22, November 2024 M4 Q20)
Re-ordering 25 − w² as (w + 5)(w − 5), or cancelling single terms instead of whole factors (Summer 2025 M4 Q20, November 2024 M4 Q19)
Inverting the second fraction and stopping — one in twenty finished the division (November 2025 M4 Q22)

workedExamples.stem: Write $\dfrac{3x}{x+5} - \dfrac{x-2}{x+1}$ as a single fraction. Give your answer with a quadratic numerator and the denominator as a product of two brackets.

steps.decision: The two denominators are different linear brackets with no factor in common, so the lowest common denominator is their product. I leave it as brackets: expanding it earns nothing and the scheme accepts either form.
Each numerator is multiplied by the other denominator. The second numerator has two terms and is being subtracted, so it stays inside a bracket until it has been expanded.

options: Because the whole of (x − 2)(x + 5) is subtracted, not only its first term
Because a numerator must always be written in brackets
whyMenu.explain: The minus sign applies to the entire product; the bracket keeps it that way until the product has been expanded.

steps.decision: Each product is expanded on its own line. The subtracted one is still inside its bracket; nothing has been removed yet.
Minus a bracket changes every sign inside it: −x², −3x, +10. This is the line the Summer 2025 examiners said most candidates lost, by subtracting only the x².

options: −10, because a constant keeps its own sign
+10, because constants are always added at the end
whyMenu.explain: Every term in the bracket is multiplied by −1, so −10 becomes +10.

steps.decision: Collect like terms: 3x² − x² = 2x², 3x − 3x = 0, and +10. The numerator shares no factor with either bracket, so this is the finished single fraction.

twin.stem: Write $\dfrac{2x}{x+3} - \dfrac{x-1}{x+2}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator.

workedExamples.stem: Write $3 + \dfrac{5}{x-2} - \dfrac{4}{2x+1}$ as a single fraction and simplify.

steps.decision: A whole number is a fraction with denominator 1, so it goes over the common denominator as well. Leaving the 3 outside is what held Summer 2024 Q18(b) to under a tenth full marks.

options: Because 3 = 3 ÷ 1, and multiplying top and bottom by (x − 2)(2x + 1) leaves its value unchanged
Because the 3 has to be added to each of the other numerators
Because whole numbers cancel with the denominators
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same expression is multiplying by 1, so the value of the 3 is unchanged.

steps.decision: All three numerators over the one denominator. The subtracted term keeps its bracket.
Expand the double bracket first, then multiply by 3. For −4(x − 2) the sign of the 8 flips: −4x + 8.
Collect: −9x + 10x − 4x = −3x and −6 + 5 + 8 = 7. The numerator does not factorise (b² − 4ac = 9 − 168 is negative), so nothing cancels.

twin.stem: Write $2 + \dfrac{3}{x+1} - \dfrac{1}{3x-2}$ as a single fraction and simplify.

steps.decision: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal, so the second fraction is turned upside down. Nothing cancels yet. The November 2025 report said most candidates inverted and then stalled: the marks are in what comes next.
A difference of two squares. The number comes first in the expression, so the brackets keep that order: (7 + y)(7 − y). Writing (y + 7)(y − 7) would give y² − 49, the negative of what we have.

options: Because (7 + y)(7 − y) = 49 − y², while (y + 7)(y − 7) = y² − 49
Because the letter should always be written second
whyMenu.explain: Expanding both shows they differ by a sign; only (7 + y)(7 − y) equals 49 − y².

steps.decision: Every numerator and denominator is factorised before anything is cancelled; each of the other three has a common factor to take out.
Cancel whole factors only: (7 − y) with (7 − y), (y + 5) with (y + 5), y with y. What remains is (7 + y) over 2.

workedExamples.stem: Solve $\dfrac{5}{x+1} + \dfrac{2}{x-3} = 2$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The left-hand side is combined over its common denominator exactly as for an expression. The = 2 waits on the right.

Both sides are multiplied by the denominator in one line: the left loses its denominator, the right becomes 2 × (x + 1)(x − 3). Every term on the right is multiplied. Summer 2024 Q23 candidates most often left the constant unmultiplied.

options: Whatever multiplies the whole of the left side must multiply the whole of the right side
The 2 is a numerator, so it collects the denominator
A denominator always moves to the other side as a divisor
whyMenu.explain: Multiplying both sides by (x + 1)(x − 3) keeps the equation balanced only if every term is multiplied.

steps.decision: The bracket product is expanded on its own line, then multiplied by 2. Brackets first, multiplier second.
Everything goes to the side that keeps x² positive: −4x − 7x = −11x and −6 + 13 = 7. Does it factorise? Pairs for 2 × 7 = 14 with sum −11: none. So the formula.
a = 2, b = −11, c = 7. Brackets around −11 before squaring: (−11)² = 121, not −121. This line is written before the calculator is touched.

options: So that −11 is squared to 121, rather than 11 squared and then negated
Because the formula sheet prints it that way
Because b is always negative in this topic
whyMenu.explain: A calculator reads −11² as −(11²) = −121; the brackets force (−11)² = 121.

steps.decision: √65 = 8.0623…, so (11 + 8.0623)/4 = 4.7656 and (11 − 8.0623)/4 = 0.7344. Both are answers: the question said solve, not find the positive value. Neither is −1 or 3, the values that would make a denominator zero.

twin.stem: Solve $\dfrac{4}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{x-1} = 2$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

items.stem: What is the common denominator for $\dfrac{3}{x+4} + \dfrac{2}{x-1}$?
items.skill: Choose the common denominator for two linear denominators

options.feedback: The two brackets share no factor, so their product is the lowest common denominator. It can be left as brackets.
The denominators were added. Fractions with different denominators are combined over the product of the denominators; adding them gives nothing a marker can credit.
One denominator on its own does not divide by the other, so the second fraction cannot be rewritten over it. Use the product of both.

items.stem: $\dfrac{5}{x-2} - \dfrac{x+3}{x+1}$ is written over $(x-2)(x+1)$. Which numerator is correct?
items.skill: Form the numerators when subtracting, keeping a two-term numerator in brackets

options.feedback: Each numerator is multiplied by the other denominator, and the subtracted product is kept inside a bracket.
The second numerator must also be multiplied, by (x − 2). Only one part of the expression was multiplied up; the method mark needs both.
Each numerator was multiplied by its own denominator. To rewrite 5/(x − 2) over (x − 2)(x + 1), multiply top and bottom by (x + 1), the factor it is missing.
The bracket around (x + 3) has been lost, so the minus reaches only the x and the 3 is multiplied on its own. Keep (x + 3)(x − 2) together inside a bracket.

items.skill: Subtract a bracketed product, changing every sign

options.feedback: Only the x² was subtracted; the 3x and the −4 kept their signs. Minus a bracket changes every term: −x² − 3x + 4.
The −4 inside the bracket becomes +4 when the bracket is removed, because −(−4) = +4.

items.skill: Put a whole number over the common denominator

options.feedback: 4 = 4(x − 1)/(x − 1), so the numerator is 4x − 4 + 3 = 4x − 1.
The 4 was added to the numerator as if it were already over (x − 1). Write it as 4(x − 1)/(x − 1) first; that is the method mark.
4(x − 1) = 4x − 4; the −4 was lost. Multiply the whole bracket, then add the 3.
Adding 4 to the top and the bottom is not how a whole number joins a fraction. Put the 4 over the denominator (x − 1).

items.skill: Factorise top and bottom and cancel a whole factor

options.feedback: (x + 3)(x − 3) over (x + 3)(x + 2); the common factor (x + 3) cancels.
The x² terms were crossed out as if they were factors. Only whole factors cancel; factorise both parts before cancelling anything.
x² − 9 = (x + 3)(x − 3). The factor shared with the denominator is (x + 3), so the bracket left on top is (x − 3).
There is no equation here. The command is simplify: factorise and cancel to a fraction; setting the expression equal to zero earns nothing.

items.skill: Difference of two squares with the number first

options.feedback: Keep the order of the expression: 6² − p² = (6 + p)(6 − p).
That expands to p² − 36, the negative of what was given. The letter does not have to come first: (6 + p)(6 − p).
(6 − p)² = 36 − 12p + p², which has a middle term. A difference of two squares has one plus bracket and one minus bracket.

options.text: It does not factorise, because the number comes first
options.feedback: It does: 36 and p² are both squares. (6 + p)(6 − p) keeps the given order and expands back to 36 − p².

items.skill: Divide by inverting the second fraction, then cancel whole brackets

options.feedback: Invert and multiply: (x + 2)/(x − 1) × (x + 5)/(x + 2); the (x + 2) brackets cancel.
Inverted and multiplied correctly, but the common factor (x + 2) has not been cancelled. Simplify means finish: cancel every whole bracket that appears top and bottom.
The x on top and bottom of (x + 5)/(x − 1) are terms, not factors, so they cannot be cancelled. The fraction (x + 5)/(x − 1) is already in its simplest form.

items.stem: For $2x^2 - 11x + 7 = 0$, which is the correct expression under the square root in the quadratic formula?
items.skill: Substitute a negative b into the formula with brackets

options.feedback: −11² means −(11²) = −121. Bracket the negative: (−11)² = 121. A negative under the root here would wrongly suggest no solutions.
The formula has −4ac. With c = +7 that is −56, not +56.
c is +7; its sign was changed. Write a = 2, b = −11, c = 7 on a line of their own before substituting.

scheme.for: common denominator (x + 1)(x + 4) with each numerator multiplied by the other denominator: 2(x + 4) + 3(x + 1)
(5x + 11) over (x + 1)(x + 4); the denominator may be left as brackets or expanded to x² + 5x + 4

hints: The denominators share no factor, so the common denominator is their product.
Multiply the 2 by (x + 4) and the 3 by (x + 1).
Expand both products, then collect: 2x + 8 + 3x + 3.
parts.workedSolution: Common denominator $(x+1)(x+4)$. Numerator $2(x+4) + 3(x+1) = 2x + 8 + 3x + 3 = 5x + 11$. So the single fraction is $\dfrac{5x+11}{(x+1)(x+4)}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Numerators and denominators were added separately. Combine over the product (x + 1)(x + 4); the method mark is for that product with the numerators multiplied up.

scheme.for: numerator expanded with the signs right: 5x + 15 − 2x + 2

hints: Common denominator (x − 1)(x + 3).
The second numerator becomes −2(x − 1); multiply both terms of the bracket by −2.

commonErrors.feedback: M1 A1 stand for the setup 5(x + 3) − 2(x − 1). Then −2 × (−1) = +2, so the numerator is 5x + 15 − 2x + 2 = 3x + 17; the final accuracy mark is lost to the sign of that 2.

hints: The common denominator is (2x + 1)(x − 2); the 2x in the first bracket changes nothing about the method.
Numerators: 4 × (x − 2) and −5 × (2x + 1).
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{4(x-2) - 5(2x+1)}{(2x+1)(x-2)} = \dfrac{4x - 8 - 10x - 5}{(2x+1)(x-2)} = \dfrac{-6x-13}{(2x+1)(x-2)}$. A negative numerator is fine; it can also be written as $-\dfrac{6x+13}{(2x+1)(x-2)}$.

commonErrors.feedback: −5 × (+1) = −5, not +5. The setup earned M1 A1; the sign on the constant costs the last mark. Write −5(2x + 1) = −10x − 5 on its own line.

parts.stem: Write $\dfrac{x}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{x-1}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator.
hints: The x on top behaves like any numerator: multiply it by the other denominator, (x − 1).
Collect the x terms: −x + 3x = 2x.

commonErrors.feedback: Adding tops and bottoms separately is not a method. Rewrite each fraction over (x + 2)(x − 1) first; that product is the method mark.

parts.stem: Write $\dfrac{2x}{x-3} - \dfrac{x+4}{x+2}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator.

scheme.for: numerators 2x(x + 2) − (x + 4)(x − 3), the subtracted product in a bracket
both products expanded, the second still inside its bracket: 2x² + 4x − (x² + x − 12)
bracket removed with every sign changed: 2x² + 4x − x² − x + 12

hints: Common denominator (x − 3)(x + 2); the second numerator (x + 4) is multiplied by (x − 3) and the whole product is subtracted.
Expand (x + 4)(x − 3) inside its bracket: x² − 3x + 4x − 12 = x² + x − 12.
Now remove the bracket: −x² − x + 12, then collect with 2x² + 4x.

commonErrors.feedback: M1 A1 MA1 earned up to the bracketed expansion. Then only the x² was subtracted: the +x and −12 must also change sign, giving 2x² + 4x − x² − x + 12. This is the slip that capped most candidates at 3 of 5 in Summer 2025.
(x + 4)(x − 3) = x² − 3x + 4x − 12 = x² + x − 12; the middle term came out as −x. M1 A1 stand and the later lines can follow through, but the accuracy of the expansion is lost.

parts.stem: Write $2 + \dfrac{3}{x+1} - \dfrac{1}{x-2}$ as a single fraction and simplify.

scheme.for: all three terms over (x + 1)(x − 2), the 2 written as 2(x + 1)(x − 2): [2(x + 1)(x − 2) + 3(x − 2) − (x + 1)] over (x + 1)(x − 2)

hints: The 2 is 2/1. Over the common denominator it becomes 2(x + 1)(x − 2).
Three numerators: 2(x + 1)(x − 2), 3(x − 2) and −(x + 1).
(x + 1)(x − 2) = x² − x − 2, so the first numerator is 2x² − 2x − 4; then collect.
parts.workedSolution:
Over the common denominator $(x+1)(x-2)$ the 2 is written as $\dfrac{2(x+1)(x-2)}{(x+1)(x-2)}$, so the numerator is $2(x+1)(x-2) + 3(x-2) - (x+1)$.
Expanded numerator: $2x^2 - 2x - 4 + 3x - 6 - x - 1$
Collected: $\dfrac{2x^2-11}{(x+1)(x-2)}$

commonErrors.feedback: The two fractions were combined correctly but the 2 was left outside, so the answer is not a single fraction. Write 2 as 2(x + 1)(x − 2) over (x + 1)(x − 2) and add its numerator to the others; only one of the two setup marks is available without it.

scheme.for: common factor out of the numerator: 3(x² − 9)
(x + 3) cancelled to give 3(x − 3) over (x − 2), or (3x − 9) over (x − 2)

hints: Take the 3 out of the numerator first: 3(x² − 9).
x² − 9 is a difference of two squares; x² + x − 6 needs two numbers with product −6 and sum 1.
Cancel the whole bracket that appears top and bottom.

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 for the 3 and MA1 for the denominator. x² − 9 still has to be factorised as (x − 3)(x + 3); without that, the (x + 3) cannot be cancelled and the last two marks go.
There is nothing to solve: the command is simplify. Factorise the numerator and the denominator, cancel the common bracket, and leave a fraction as the answer.

scheme.for: numerator factorised in the order given: (4 + t)(4 − t)
(4 + t) recognised as (t + 4) and cancelled: (4 − t) over (t + 2); accept −(t − 4) over (t + 2)

hints: 16 − t² is 4² − t²: a difference of two squares with the number first.
(4 + t)(4 − t) keeps the given order; (t + 4)(t − 4) would be t² − 16.
(4 + t) and (t + 4) are the same bracket, so they cancel.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{(4+t)(4-t)}{(t+2)(t+4)} = \dfrac{4-t}{t+2}$, because $(4+t)$ and $(t+4)$ are the same factor.

commonErrors.feedback: (t + 4)(t − 4) is t² − 16, the negative of the numerator, so the answer has the wrong sign. MA1 for the denominator stands; keep the order 4² − t² = (4 + t)(4 − t), cancel (4 + t) with (t + 4), and the answer is (4 − t)/(t + 2).

scheme.for: numerator grouped in pairs with a common bracket: a(b + 3) + 2(b + 3)

hints: Four terms on top: group them in pairs, ab + 3a and 2b + 6.
a(b + 3) + 2(b + 3) has the bracket (b + 3) in both parts, so it is (a + 2)(b + 3).
a² − 4 is a difference of two squares.

commonErrors.feedback: An a was crossed out of ab and of a². Those are terms inside sums, not factors of the whole numerator and denominator, so nothing has been simplified and no mark is available. Factorise by grouping first.

hints: Multiplying fractions: tops together, bottoms together — but factorise everything before you multiply anything.
Cancel (x − 2) top and bottom, and (x + 4) top and bottom.

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 MA1 for the factorising done so far. x² − 2x = x(x − 2); without that the (x − 2) on top has nothing to cancel with and the answer is not fully simplified.

scheme.for: second fraction inverted and the operation changed to multiply: (2x + 6)/(x² − 1) × (x + 1)/(x² + 3x)
(x + 3) and (x + 1) cancelled: 2 over x(x − 1), or 2 over x² − x

hints: Turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.
Factorise all four parts: 2(x + 3), (x + 1)(x − 1), x(x + 3), and (x + 1) is already a factor.
Cancel (x + 3) with (x + 3) and (x + 1) with (x + 1).

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 for inverting. Nothing can cancel until every numerator and denominator is factorised: 2(x + 3), (x + 1)(x − 1), x(x + 3). Then the (x + 3) and (x + 1) brackets go and 2 over x(x − 1) is left. November 2025: one in twenty finished this kind of item.

scheme.for: denominators cleared with every term multiplied: 4x − 2 = 2(x + 1)(x − 1) = 2x² − 2

hints: Combine the left-hand side over (x + 1)(x − 1) first; the = 2 waits.
Multiply both sides by (x + 1)(x − 1): 4x − 2 = 2(x² − 1).
2x² − 4x = 0 has a common factor 2x; do not divide by x, or a solution disappears.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{3(x-1) + (x+1)}{(x+1)(x-1)} = 2 \Rightarrow 4x - 2 = 2(x^2 - 1) \Rightarrow 2x^2 - 4x = 0 \Rightarrow 2x(x-2) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 2$. Neither value makes a denominator zero.

commonErrors.feedback: M1 A1 for combining the left side. Then the right-hand 2 was not multiplied by (x + 1)(x − 1): the line should read 4x − 2 = 2(x + 1)(x − 1). Multiply every term on both sides in one line.
x = 2 is right, but 2x(x − 2) = 0 also gives x = 0, which satisfies the equation. Dividing through by x threw a solution away; the final accuracy mark needs both.

parts.stem: Solve $\dfrac{5}{2x-1} - \dfrac{3}{x+2} = 1$. Give your answers to 2 decimal places.
hints: Combine the left side: 5(x + 2) − 3(2x − 1) over (2x − 1)(x + 2). The −3 multiplies both terms of (2x − 1).
Multiply both sides by (2x − 1)(x + 2), then expand (2x − 1)(x + 2) on its own line.
Collect to 2x² + 4x − 15 = 0. It does not factorise, so use the formula with a = 2, b = 4, c = −15, and give both roots.

commonErrors.feedback: −3(2x − 1) = −6x + 3, not −6x − 3. M1 A1 for the setup, and the later method can follow through from 2x² + 4x − 9 = 0, but the expansion mark and the final accuracy are lost.
Six of the seven marks stand. The formula gave a second root, −3.92, and nothing in the question rules it out; the answer line needs both values.

parts.stem:
Solve

$\dfrac{2x}{x+3} + \dfrac{3}{x-2} = \dfrac{5}{2}$

Give both answers correct to 2 decimal places.
hints: Combine the left side over (x + 3)(x − 2); the 2x on top is multiplied by (x − 2).
You now have a fraction equal to 5/2: cross-multiply, so 2 × (numerator) = 5 × (denominator).
4x² − 2x + 18 = 5x² + 5x − 30 collects to x² + 7x − 48 = 0; the formula with a = 1, b = 7, c = −48.

commonErrors.feedback: Seven of the eight marks stand. The second root, −11.26, is a solution too; the question said solve, so both go on the answer line. November 2024: candidates again ignored the negative root.
3(x + 3) = 3x + 9; the 3 must multiply both terms. M1 A1 stand and the method follows through, but the numerator 2x² − x + 3 costs the expansion mark and both accuracy marks.

parts.stem:
An expression is written as

$\dfrac{3x}{x-4} - \dfrac{x+2}{x+3}$

Write the expression as a single fraction. Give your answer with a quadratic numerator and with the denominator as a product of two brackets.

scheme.for: numerators 3x(x + 3) − (x + 2)(x − 4), the subtracted product in a bracket
bracket removed with every sign changed: 3x² + 9x − x² + 2x + 8

scheme.examinerNote: 2x² + 7x − 8 (only the x² subtracted) scores M1 A1 MA1 at most.

hints: Common denominator (x − 4)(x + 3); the second numerator (x + 2) is multiplied by (x − 4) and the whole product is subtracted.
(x + 2)(x − 4) = x² − 4x + 2x − 8 = x² − 2x − 8; keep it in a bracket.
Removing the bracket: −x² + 2x + 8; then collect with 3x² + 9x.

commonErrors.feedback: M1 A1 MA1 up to the bracketed expansion. Only the x² was subtracted after that; −2x and −8 must change sign too, giving 3x² + 9x − x² + 2x + 8. The Summer 2025 report: this capped most candidates at 3.
(x + 2)(x − 4) = x² − 2x − 8; the middle term came out as +2x. The setup marks stand and the sign change was done correctly afterwards, so 3 of 5.

hints: Fully means every common factor first: both terms divide by 5 and by b.
x² − 9y² is a difference of two squares: (3y)² = 9y².

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 for 5b. The bracket is a difference of two squares and fully means it must be factorised too: (x + 3y)(x − 3y).
Only the 5 was taken out; b is a factor of both terms as well. Without 5b the difference of two squares cannot be seen, and the scheme's first mark is for 5b(x² − 9y²).

scheme.for: second fraction inverted and the other three parts factorised: 5b(x + 3y)(x − 3y)/(4x(x + 3y)) × 2x(x − 3)/(10b²)

hints: Hence: the numerator of the first fraction is your answer to (a). Turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.
4x² + 12xy = 4x(x + 3y) and 2x² − 6x = 2x(x − 3).
Cancel (x + 3y) with (x + 3y), x with x, and one b with b²; then 5 × 2 ÷ (4 × 10) = 1/4.

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 for inverting and using part (a). The remaining parts must be factorised before anything cancels: 4x(x + 3y) and 2x(x − 3); then (x + 3y), x and b go. November 2025: one in twenty finished.

scheme.for: numerator grouped and factorised: 3(4 + m) + k(4 + m) = (4 + m)(3 + k)
common factor out of the denominator: 2(16 − m²)
difference of two squares in the order given: 2(4 + m)(4 − m)
(4 + m) cancelled: (3 + k) over 2(4 − m); accept (k + 3) over (8 − 2m)
scheme.examinerNote: (3 + k) over 2(m − 4) has the wrong sign and does not earn this mark.

hints: Four terms on top: 12 + 3m and 4k + km each have a common factor, and the brackets left behind match.
32 − 2m² = 2(16 − m²), and 16 − m² is 4² − m².
Write (4 + m)(4 − m), not (m + 4)(m − 4), and cancel the (4 + m).

commonErrors.feedback: 16 − m² was written as (m + 4)(m − 4), which is m² − 16: the sign of the whole denominator has flipped, so the answer is the negative of the correct one. MA1 MA1 for the numerator and the 2; keep the order 4² − m² = (4 + m)(4 − m).

Nothing has been simplified: crossing out an m from 3m and 2m², or a 4 from 4k and 32, changes the value because those are terms inside sums. Factorise both parts, then cancel the whole bracket (4 + m).

parts.stem:
Solve the equation

$\dfrac{5}{x-2} - \dfrac{3}{x+3} = 1$

Give your answers to 2 decimal places.

scheme.for: formula substituted with the negative b bracketed: x = (1 ± √((−1)² − 4(1)(−27))) ÷ 2

hints: Combine the left side over (x − 2)(x + 3): 5(x + 3) − 3(x − 2). The −3 multiplies both terms.
Multiply both sides by (x − 2)(x + 3) in one line; the 1 on the right becomes (x − 2)(x + 3).
x² − x − 27 = 0 does not factorise (pairs for −27 with sum −1: none), so the formula with a = 1, b = −1, c = −27.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{5(x+3) - 3(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+3)} = 1 \Rightarrow 2x + 21 = x^2 + x - 6 \Rightarrow x^2 - x - 27 = 0$. $x = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 108}}{2} = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{109}}{2}$, so $x = 5.72$ or $x = -4.72$ (2 d.p.). Neither is 2 or −3, so both stand.

commonErrors.feedback: −3(x − 2) = −3x + 6, not −3x − 6. M1 A1 for the setup and the method follows through from x² − x − 15 = 0, but the expansion mark and the final accuracy are gone. Write the expansion of each bracket on its own line.
b = −1, so b² = (−1)² = 1; typed as −1² the calculator gives −1 and the discriminant becomes 107 instead of 109. Five marks stand; bracket (−b) before squaring.
Six of seven. The formula also gave −4.72, which satisfies the equation; with no context to exclude it, both roots belong on the answer line.

context.setting: A cyclist rides 12 km to the coast and back, the return journey 5 km/h faster, 2 hours in total

parts.stem:
Aoife cycles 12 km from home to the coast at an average speed of $x$ km/h. She cycles home by the same road at an average speed 5 km/h faster. The two journeys take 2 hours altogether.

Form an equation in $x$ and show that it simplifies to $x^2 - 7x - 30 = 0$.

scheme.for: time = distance ÷ speed used for at least one journey: 12/x or 12/(x + 5)
denominators cleared with every term multiplied: 12(x + 5) + 12x = 2x(x + 5)
24x + 60 = 2x² + 10x, then divided by 2 and rearranged to the printed equation with the working shown
scheme.examinerNote: The line before the printed result must be seen; starting from x² − 7x − 30 = 0 earns nothing.

hints: Time = distance ÷ speed. Write the time for each journey as a fraction in x.
The two times add to 2 hours: 12/x + 12/(x + 5) = 2.
Multiply every term by x(x + 5), collect on one side, and divide by 2.
parts.workedSolution: Times: $\dfrac{12}{x}$ and $\dfrac{12}{x+5}$ hours, so $\dfrac{12}{x} + \dfrac{12}{x+5} = 2$. Multiply by $x(x+5)$: $12(x+5) + 12x = 2x(x+5)$, so $24x + 60 = 2x^2 + 10x$, so $2x^2 - 14x - 60 = 0$ and, dividing by 2, $x^2 - 7x - 30 = 0$.

commonErrors.feedback: Solving the printed equation is not what part (a) asks. Show that means start from the journey times, form 12/x + 12/(x + 5) = 2, and work forward to the quadratic; the marks are for that chain.
M1 A1 for the times and the equation. When both sides are multiplied by x(x + 5), the 2 must be multiplied too: 12(x + 5) + 12x = 2x(x + 5).

parts.stem: Solve the equation to find Aoife's average speed on the journey to the coast.

scheme.for: (x − 10)(x + 3) = 0, or the formula with a = 1, b = −7, c = −30
10 km/h, with −3 rejected because a speed cannot be negative
scheme.examinerNote: Both values left on the answer line score 2.

hints: Pairs with product −30 and sum −7: −10 and +3.
(x − 10)(x + 3) = 0 gives two values.
One of them is not a possible speed. Say why, and give the other with its unit.
parts.workedSolution: $x^2 - 7x - 30 = (x-10)(x+3) = 0$, so $x = 10$ or $x = -3$. A speed cannot be negative, so $x = -3$ is rejected: Aoife's speed to the coast was 10 km/h.

commonErrors.feedback: MA1 A1 for both roots. The context decides: −3 km/h is not a speed, so it is rejected with that reason and 10 km/h is the answer. Leaving both values costs the final mark.
(x + 10)(x − 3) expands to x² + 7x − 30, not x² − 7x − 30. Check a factorisation by expanding the middle term: −10x + 3x = −7x.

methodLock.instruction: Form an equation and show that
methodLock.requiredMethod: Algebraic derivation from the journey times; trial and improvement or working backwards from the printed equation earns no marks

findTheMistake.stem: Cara was asked to write $\dfrac{4x}{x+1} - \dfrac{x-3}{x+2}$ as a single fraction with a quadratic numerator. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: (x − 3)(x + 1) = x² − 2x − 3, and the whole of it is subtracted. Cara subtracted only the x²: the −2x and −3 kept their signs instead of becoming +2x and +3.
findTheMistake.feedback: M1 A1 for the common denominator and the correctly bracketed numerators. Line 3 is where the marks stop: the product was never shown inside its bracket, so the sign change was applied to one term only. Expand inside the bracket on one line, remove it on the next with every sign changed, then collect. Summer 2025 M4 Q21: this slip capped most candidates at 3 of 5.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara was asked to solve $\dfrac{4}{x-1} - \dfrac{3}{x+2} = 1$, giving his answers to 2 decimal places. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Multiplying by (x − 1)(x + 2) removed the denominator on the left, but the 1 on the right was not multiplied. The right-hand side should be (x − 1)(x + 2), which is why the quadratic never appeared.
findTheMistake.feedback: M1 A1 for combining the left-hand side. From line 2 nothing more can be credited: an equation with two algebraic denominators must produce a quadratic, and a linear answer is the signal to look back. A check would also have caught it: at x = −10 the left side is 4/(−11) − 3/(−8) ≈ 0.01, not 1. Summer 2024 M4 Q23: the constant on the other side was the term most often left unmultiplied.

findTheMistake.stem: Eimear was solving $\dfrac{3}{x-2} + \dfrac{1}{x+1} = 1$, giving her answers to 2 decimal places. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: b = −5, so b² is (−5)² = 25. Written as −5² the calculator squares 5 and then makes it negative, giving −25, so the discriminant came out as −13 instead of 25 + 12 = 37.
findTheMistake.feedback: Lines 1–4 are correct: M1 A1 for the setup, MA1 for clearing the denominators, MA1 for the quadratic. The formula line loses its mark and the final accuracy with it, 4 of 7. Bracket the negative before squaring, (−5)², and write the substitution before pressing anything. In this topic a negative under the root is almost always a slip to hunt for, not a conclusion. November 2025 M4 Q24: b² without brackets was the reported cause.

prompts.prompt: The four moves for writing a/(x + p) ± b/(x + q) as a single fraction.
prompts.answer: 1 Common denominator (x + p)(x + q). 2 Multiply each numerator by the other denominator, keeping a subtracted numerator in brackets. 3 Expand, then change every sign inside a subtracted bracket. 4 Collect like terms and leave the denominator as brackets.

prompts.prompt: A numerator reads $5x^2 + 2x - (x^2 - 4x - 7)$. What does it become when the bracket is removed?
prompts.answer: $5x^2 + 2x - x^2 + 4x + 7 = 4x^2 + 6x + 7$. Every sign inside the bracket changes, not only the first.

prompts.prompt: How is a whole number, say 3, combined with fractions whose common denominator is (x − 2)(2x + 1)?
prompts.answer: Write it as 3(x − 2)(2x + 1) over (x − 2)(2x + 1), then add its numerator to the others. A whole number is a fraction with denominator 1.

prompts.prompt: Can $\dfrac{x^2 + 5}{x^2 + 3x}$ be simplified by cancelling the $x^2$ terms?
prompts.answer: No. Only whole factors cancel; x² is a term of each expression, not a factor of it. Factorise first: the denominator is x(x + 3), the numerator has no common factor, so nothing cancels.
$(8 + k)(8 - k)$. Keep the order given: $(k + 8)(k - 8)$ is $k^2 - 64$, the negative.

prompts.prompt: Dividing one algebraic fraction by another: the three moves.
prompts.answer: Invert the second fraction and multiply; factorise every numerator and denominator (common factor, difference of two squares, grouping); cancel whole brackets and write the single fraction that remains.

prompts.prompt: Solving a/(x + p) + b/(x + q) = c: the moves in order.
prompts.answer: Combine the left side over (x + p)(x + q); multiply both sides by that denominator in one line, every term on the right included; expand the bracket product on its own line; collect into ax² + bx + c = 0; factorise if possible, otherwise the formula with (−b)² bracketed; give both roots to the accuracy asked and check that neither makes a denominator zero.

prompts.prompt: In the quadratic formula with b = −9, what is b²?
prompts.answer: (−9)² = 81. Typed as −9², a calculator gives −81 and the discriminant comes out wrong, often negative.

prompts.prompt: A fractional equation with no context gives x = 4.26 and x = −11.26. The question said solve. What goes on the answer line?
prompts.answer: Both values. A root is rejected only when a context forbids it (a negative speed or length) or it makes a denominator zero, and then the reason is written down.

prompts.prompt: Which denominators are in scope for adding, subtracting and solving on M4, and which are excluded?
prompts.answer: Linear denominators such as x + 2, 2x − 1 or x, including a numerical one alongside. The Teacher Guidance excludes quadratic denominators from both the addition statement and the equation statement.

prompts.prompt: Which of these is printed on the Higher formula sheet: the quadratic formula, the difference of two squares, the rule for dividing fractions?
prompts.answer: Only the quadratic formula. a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) and invert-and-multiply must be known.

findings.asked: Solve an equation with two algebraic fractions that leads to a quadratic.
findings.wentWrong: Only the more able finished. Errors when expanding brackets and collecting terms, dropping the negative root, and not rounding to 2 d.p. Weaker candidates could not start.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Combined the fractions over a common denominator, cross-multiplied to a quadratic, solved with the formula and gave both roots to 2 d.p.
findings.rule: Both roots count unless the context rules one out; round only at the end.

findings.asked: Write two algebraic fractions and a whole number as a single fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Under a tenth got full marks. Most combined the two fractions but had no idea what to do with the whole number.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the whole number as (number x common denominator) / common denominator and combined all three numerators.
findings.rule: A whole number is a fraction with denominator 1 - put it over the common denominator too.

findings.asked: Solve an equation where the unknown is in the denominators.
findings.wentWrong: About a fifth got full marks. Common denominator and cross-multiplying were known, but the constant term was mishandled, fractions were moved across with wrong signs, and tidying up went wrong; most still reached a quadratic for some credit.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept every term over one denominator, expanded carefully, and solved their quadratic (follow-through was available once most of the setup marks were earned and the roots were real).
findings.rule: Clear the denominators in one line, then expand with brackets before simplifying.

findings.asked: A standard fractional equation leading to a quadratic, with all the algebra on one side.
findings.wentWrong: One in five got full marks; most got the first two marks, then made errors expanding brackets and handling the constants. Some again ignored the negative root.
findings.rule: Write the expansion of every bracket as a separate line before collecting terms.

findings.asked: Add two algebraic fractions and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: Most got the common denominator and the first line, then subtracted only the first term of a multi-term numerator, capping them at 3 marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the subtracted numerator in brackets, expanded it fully with the sign applied to every term, then collected.
findings.rule: Minus a bracket changes every sign inside it.

findings.asked: Solve a fractional equation with algebraic denominators.
findings.wentWrong: Only top candidates finished; most set up the left-hand side correctly. Negative numbers caused trouble in expansions such as a multiple of (p - 1), and negative b was squared without brackets inside the quadratic formula.
findings.rule: Type (-b) in brackets when squaring in the quadratic formula.

findings.asked: Factorise the numerator and denominator of an algebraic fraction and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: About a third got full marks. Most took the common factor 2 out (some just divided by 2 instead), then partial credit for a difference of two squares. Weaker candidates cancelled single terms across the fraction or tried to solve it as an equation.
findings.rule: Only common factors cancel; an expression is simplified, never solved.

findings.asked: Factorise (grouping in the numerator, difference of two squares in the denominator) and cancel.
findings.wentWrong: Most got a mark for taking 3 out of the denominator. The difference of two squares went wrong when the letter was not the first term, because candidates swapped the terms round; grouping in the numerator troubled the less able.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the terms in their given order, wrote a squared minus b squared as (a + b)(a - b), and cancelled whole brackets.
findings.rule: 25 - w squared factorises as (5 + w)(5 - w) - do not reorder.

findings.asked: Divide one algebraic fraction by another and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: Only one in twenty finished. Most earned a mark or two for inverting the second fraction and factorising the denominators, then stalled.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Inverted, factorised every numerator and denominator, cancelled the common brackets, and wrote the single remaining fraction.
findings.rule: Flip, factorise everything, cancel whole brackets.

insight.ruleToRemember: Put every term - including whole numbers - over the common denominator, keep subtracted numerators in brackets, cross-multiply to a quadratic, then give both roots (rejecting one only with a reason) rounded at the very end.
insight.aStarSignal: The unknown in two denominators with a constant elsewhere: cleared in one line, expanded without sign slips, and solved with the formula to 2 d.p. with both roots stated.
